Cialdini's later research on pre-suasion shows that what happens just before a request matters: directing someone's attention to a particular idea makes them more receptive to related requests. He insists on ethical use: the principles should be used to point out genuine features of a situation, not to manufacture false ones. If the scarcity is real, say so. If the expert is genuine, introduce them.
practice: Compliance and leadership work depend on influence without force. Social proof works when you share that most comparable institutions have already adopted a control. Commitment works when people write down their own action points. Reciprocity works when you help a department before asking for its cooperation. Unity works when you frame a request as 'we' rather than 'compliance versus business'. The same principles also help you recognise when someone is using them on you.
faith: Good and evil are not equal. Repel evil with that which is better, and the one between whom and you was enmity will become as though he were a devoted friend. This is the deepest form of influence: reciprocity elevated to ihsan, returning harm with good. Ibn Kathir notes that Ibn 'Abbas explained it as patience when angered and forgiveness when wronged, and that when people do this, Allah protects them and their enemies yield to them. The Prophet, peace be upon him, won hearts this way, as when he forgave the people of Makkah on the day of its opening.
nigerian: The Igbo say «Onye wetara ọjị wetara ndụ»: he who brings kola brings life. Hospitality and generosity open doors in Nigerian culture long before business is discussed. Reciprocity is woven into our customs, which is why it must never be turned into a tool of manipulation or bribery.
practices: Before asking a colleague for support, help them with something first, sincerely.
In your next proposal, use honest social proof: what have similar institutions done?
When someone pressures you with urgency or a gift, pause and ask which principle is being used.
reflect: Which principle do I rely on most, and do I use it honestly?
Is there someone whose hostility I could repel with something better?
closing: Influence is a trust. Use it truthfully, never to manipulate, and remember the highest form: repel evil with what is better.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَسْتَوِى ٱلْحَسَنَةُ وَلَا ٱلسَّيِّئَةُ ٱدْفَعْ بِٱلَّتِى هِىَ أَحْسَنُ فَإِذَا ٱلَّذِى بَيْنَكَ وَبَيْنَهُۥ عَدَٰوَةٌ كَأَنَّهُۥ وَلِىٌّ حَمِيمٌ
verses.en: And not equal are the good deed and the bad. Repel [evil] by that [deed] which is better; and thereupon, the one whom between you and him is enmity [will become] as though he was a devoted friend.

title: Give and Take
tag: Givers finish both last and first. The difference is how they give.
source: Adam Grant, Give and Take (2013); 'In the Company of Givers and Takers', Harvard Business Review (2013)
opening: Adam Grant became the youngest tenured professor at the Wharton School partly through research on a simple question: in the workplace, do generous people succeed or fail? The answer turned out to be both.
idea: Grant identifies three reciprocity styles. Takers try to get more than they give, putting their own interests first. Matchers try to keep an even balance: I help you, you help me. Givers contribute to others without expecting anything in return. When Grant looked at performance data, from engineers to salespeople to medical students, givers were overrepresented at the bottom: they were exploited, burned out and fell behind. But givers were also overrepresented at the very top. Takers and matchers tended to land in the middle. The question is what separates the givers who succeed from the givers who are trampled.
mechanics: Successful givers are what Grant calls 'otherish': they care about others, but they also have ambitious goals for themselves. Selfless givers sacrifice their own interests to the point of exhaustion. Otherish givers give in ways that also energise them, chunk their giving into concentrated blocks rather than constant interruptions, and protect time for their own work. They are also not naive. They begin by trusting, but they learn to recognise takers, and adopt a 'generous tit for tat' with them: mostly matching, but occasionally forgiving. Grant also found that givers build networks that grow in value over time, because people remember who helped them, and that the five-minute favour, a small act of help like an introduction or a piece of advice, has outsized effects.
practice: Organisations benefit most from cultures where people help each other, seek help freely, and where takers are screened out. Grant notes that one taker on a team can do more damage than several givers can repair. Leaders should reward collaboration, make help-seeking normal, and protect their best givers from burnout.
faith: And they give preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul, it is those who will be the successful. This verse describes the Ansar of Madinah, who shared their homes and wealth with the migrants from Makkah. Ithar, preferring others, is the highest form of giving. Yet the Prophet, peace be upon him, also taught balance: he told Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas not to give away more than a third of his wealth in his will, saying it is better to leave your heirs wealthy than dependent on others, in a hadith in both Sahihs. Generous, but wise. Otherish.
nigerian: Nigerian social life is built on giving: extended family support, contributions at ceremonies, the obligations that come with success. Grant's research helps here. Giving that is chunked, chosen and sustainable builds influence and blessing; giving without boundaries leads to burnout and resentment.
practices: Do one five-minute favour each day this week: an introduction, a word of advice, or a quick review.
Choose one block of time each week for helping others, and protect the rest for your own priorities.
Identify one taker relationship in your life, and set a clear, kind boundary.
reflect: Am I a giver, a matcher or a taker at work? At home?
Is my giving otherish or selfless to the point of harm?
closing: Give generously, prefer others, and be protected from the stinginess of the soul, but give wisely, so that you can keep giving for a lifetime.

verses.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ تَبَوَّءُو ٱلدَّارَ وَٱلْإِيمَٰنَ مِن قَبْلِهِمْ يُحِبُّونَ مَنْ هَاجَرَ إِلَيْهِمْ وَلَا يَجِدُونَ فِى صُدُورِهِمْ حَاجَةً مِّمَّآ أُوتُوا۟ وَيُؤْثِرُونَ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِهِمْ وَلَوْ كَانَ بِهِمْ خَصَاصَةٌ وَمَن يُوقَ شُحَّ نَفْسِهِۦ فَأُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ هُمُ ٱلْمُفْلِحُونَ
verses.en: And [also for] those who were settled in the Home [i.e.,al-Madīnah] and [adopted] the faith before them. They love those who emigrated to them and find not any want in their breasts of what they [i.e., the emigrants] were given but give [them] preference over themselves, even though they are in privation. And whoever is protected from the stinginess of his soul - it is those who will be the successful.

title: Social Capital & Networks
tag: Relationships are capital, and the weak ties often matter most.
source: Mark Granovetter, 'The Strength of Weak Ties', American Journal of Sociology (1973); Robert Putnam, Making Democracy Work (1993) and Bowling Alone (2000)
hadith: Whoever would like his provision to be expanded and his life to be extended, let him maintain the ties of kinship.
Sahih al-Bukhari 5986, Sahih Muslim 2557
opening: In 1973 the sociologist Mark Granovetter published a paper with a paradoxical title: The Strength of Weak Ties. It became one of the most cited papers in social science. Two decades later, Robert Putnam of Harvard showed that the health of entire societies depends on the relationships between their citizens.
idea: Granovetter studied how people found jobs, and discovered that most found them not through close friends but through acquaintances, people they saw only occasionally. Strong ties, close friends and family, tend to know the same people and the same information you do. Weak ties connect you to different circles, bringing new information and opportunities. Putnam developed the idea of social capital: the networks, norms and trust that enable people to cooperate. In his study of Italian regions, he found that areas with dense civic associations, choirs, clubs and cooperatives, had far better governments and economies. In Bowling Alone, he documented the collapse of such ties in America and its cost to trust, health and democracy.
mechanics: Putnam distinguishes bonding social capital, which ties similar people together, such as family, ethnic or religious groups, from bridging social capital, which connects different groups. Bonding provides support and identity, but on its own can become exclusive or even hostile to outsiders. Bridging builds wider trust and opportunity. A healthy person and a healthy society need both. Later network research, such as Ronald Burt's work on structural holes, showed that people who bridge gaps between otherwise disconnected groups tend to have better ideas and faster careers, because they see combinations others cannot.
practice: For a professional working across several companies, regulators and communities, the network is an asset to be cultivated deliberately and ethically. That means maintaining weak ties with occasional, genuine contact, introducing people to each other, and building bridges between sectors. It also means guarding against the dark side of networks: favouritism, conflicts of interest and nepotism, which are the bonding ties of social capital gone wrong.
faith: O mankind, We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allah is the most righteous. Diversity is created for ta'aruf, mutual knowing: bridging capital as a divine purpose. And the Prophet, peace be upon him, linked maintaining kinship ties with expanded provision and a longer life, bonding capital as an act of worship. Islam joins both: strong roots in family, and open bridges to all of humanity, with righteousness, not tribe, as the measure.
nigerian: The Hausa say «Da ɗan gari ake cin gari»: you conquer a town with the help of its own people. Nigeria's diversity of more than two hundred and fifty ethnic groups is either a source of division or an enormous bridging network. The leaders who thrive are those whose relationships cross region, religion and sector.
practices: Contact three weak ties this week with no request, only a genuine greeting or useful piece of information.
Introduce two people in your network who could help each other.
Visit or call one relative you have neglected, for the sake of Allah.
reflect: Are my relationships mostly bonding, or do I also build bridges?
Where might my network create a conflict of interest I should guard against?
closing: Know one another, maintain your ties, and build bridges. Relationships are provision, and Allah has linked them to the blessing in your sustenance and your life.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلنَّاسُ إِنَّا خَلَقْنَٰكُم مِّن ذَكَرٍ وَأُنثَىٰ وَجَعَلْنَٰكُمْ شُعُوبًا وَقَبَآئِلَ لِتَعَارَفُوٓا۟ إِنَّ أَكْرَمَكُمْ عِندَ ٱللَّهِ أَتْقَىٰكُمْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌ
verses.en: O mankind, indeed We have created you from male and female and made you peoples and tribes that you may know one another. Indeed, the most noble of you in the sight of Allāh is the most righteous of you. Indeed, Allāh is Knowing and Aware.

title: Adaptive Leadership
tag: Most failures of leadership come from treating adaptive challenges as technical problems.
source: Ronald Heifetz and Marty Linsky, Leadership on the Line (2002); Heifetz, Grashow and Linsky, The Practice of Adaptive Leadership (2009)
opening: For more than three decades Ronald Heifetz has taught one of the most demanding leadership courses at Harvard's Kennedy School. His central claim is simple and uncomfortable: the hardest problems leaders face cannot be solved by the leader. They can only be solved by the people who have the problem.
idea: Heifetz separates two kinds of challenge. A technical problem has a known solution and an expert who can apply it: a broken pipe, a missing report template, a system upgrade. An adaptive challenge has no ready answer, because solving it requires people to change their own values, habits, loyalties or beliefs. A culture of late reporting, a family business moving to professional management, a team that hides errors from the regulator: these are adaptive. The most common failure of leadership, he argues, is treating an adaptive challenge as if it were technical, issuing a new policy or hiring a consultant, while the real work, which is a change in people, never begins.
mechanics: Adaptive work always involves loss. People are asked to give up something they value: status, comfort, a familiar way of working, an identity. So they resist, and they push the pain back onto the leader. Heifetz gives leaders several disciplines. Get on the balcony: step out of the dance floor of daily action and observe the patterns, including your own part in them. Regulate the heat: keep the pressure high enough that people engage, but not so high that they panic or rebel, like a pressure cooker that must neither go cold nor explode. Give the work back: resist the temptation to solve it yourself, because people only adapt when they carry the responsibility. And protect the voices of leadership without authority, the junior officer or the outsider who names the uncomfortable truth.
practice: Heifetz also distinguishes authority from leadership. Authority is the formal power you are given: a title, a budget, a seat on the committee. Leadership is the act of mobilising people to face hard reality, and it is often done without authority, or even at its expense. That is why he warns that leading is dangerous. When you ask people to face loss, they try to neutralise you: by marginalising you, diverting attention, attacking you personally, or seducing you into the comfortable role they prefer. Survival depends on not taking the attacks personally, on keeping allies and confidants separate, and on anchoring yourself in a purpose larger than the role.
faith: Allah does not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves. Ibn Kathir explains this as a law of Allah's dealings with nations: blessings and hardships follow the inner state of people. This is the deepest statement of adaptive work. No decree from above, no new policy, replaces the change people must make within. The Prophet, peace be upon him, spent thirteen years in Makkah building inner conviction before outward structures came in Madinah. He gave the work back to his companions, trained them, consulted them, and let them carry the change.
nigerian: The Yoruba say «Ìkòkò tí yóò jẹ ata, ìdí rẹ̀ á gbóná»: the pot that will cook pepper must have its bottom heated. Real change in our institutions requires heat. The late Dora Akunyili, who led NAFDAC's campaign against fake drugs, met attacks and even an attempt on her life, yet she kept the pressure on long enough for public expectations to shift.
practices: List the three biggest problems in your unit and label each technical or adaptive.
For one adaptive challenge, name what each group would have to lose for it to be solved.
Spend ten minutes after each major meeting 'on the balcony', writing what patterns you saw, including your own role.
reflect: Where am I solving a problem myself that my team must learn to carry?
What loss am I asking people to accept, and have I acknowledged it?
closing: Technical problems need experts. Adaptive challenges need leaders who can hold people in productive discomfort until they change. Allah has told us where change begins: within.

verses.ar: لَهُۥ مُعَقِّبَٰتٌ مِّنۢ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِۦ يَحْفَظُونَهُۥ مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ وَإِذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ سُوٓءًا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُۥ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَالٍ
verses.en: For him [i.e., each one] are successive [angels] before and behind him who protect him by the decree of Allāh. Indeed, Allāh will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allāh intends for a people ill, there is no repelling it. And there is not for them besides Him any patron.

title: True North
tag: Authentic leaders are formed in their crucibles, not their comfort.
source: Bill George, True North (2007, revised 2015); George et al., 'Discovering Your Authentic Leadership', Harvard Business Review (2007)
opening: When Bill George, the former chief executive of Medtronic, joined Harvard Business School as a professor, he and his colleagues interviewed 125 leaders to find what made them effective. They expected to find a set of traits. They found something else.
idea: There was no common profile. No single set of characteristics, style or personality predicted great leadership. What these leaders shared was an understanding of their own life story, and a willingness to lead from it. George called this a true north: an internal compass made of your values, your purpose and the lessons of your experience, which keeps you on course when external pressures, money, fame or fear, pull you off. Leaders who lose their true north, he argued, are the ones who end in scandal, because they begin to chase external validation.
mechanics: The most important parts of a leader's story are crucibles: experiences of hardship, failure or loss that test them to the core. A dismissal, an illness, the death of a parent, a public failure. George found that the leaders who grew most were those who processed their crucibles honestly, instead of hiding them. He recommends practices to develop self-awareness, such as reflection, journaling, prayer or meditation, and honest feedback from a small support team of people who will tell you the truth. He also distinguishes intrinsic motivations, such as personal growth and making a difference, from extrinsic ones, such as status and money. Leaders who are driven mostly by the extrinsic tend to make choices that look good but feel empty.
practice: George describes the leader's path in three phases: preparing for leadership, leading, and a final phase of giving back. He also warns of the danger of becoming a 'loser of the self', a leader so shaped by the expectations of the role that he no longer knows what he believes. The defence is a coherent life in which the person at work, at home and in the community is the same person. For someone carrying several roles across several companies, this is the key question: is there one person underneath all the titles?
faith: So truly, with hardship comes ease. Truly, with hardship comes ease. The scholars note that 'hardship' is definite and repeated, while 'ease' is indefinite, so one hardship is followed by more than one ease. Ibn Kathir records the saying that one hardship will not overcome two eases. Every prophet had a crucible: Yusuf in the well and the prison, Musa in exile, the Prophet, peace be upon him, at Ta'if, bleeding and rejected. Each came out with a clearer sense of mission. Your crucibles are not interruptions to your leadership. They are where it is forged.
nigerian: Chinua Achebe wrote Things Fall Apart partly in response to a European picture of Africa he knew to be false. His true north was the conviction that a people must tell their own story. Leaders who know their story, and are not ashamed of it, lead with an authority no title can give.
practices: Write the three crucibles of your life in a page each: what happened, what you felt, and what it taught you.
Name your three core values, and one decision this month that tested each.
Identify two or three people who will tell you the truth about yourself, and ask them for it.
reflect: Am I the same person in every role I hold?
Which motivation drives me more, the intrinsic or the extrinsic?
closing: Your compass is not in your title. It is in your values, your purpose, and the lessons Allah has written into your life through hardship and ease.

verses.ar: فَإِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
verses.en: For indeed, with hardship [will be] ease [i.e., relief].

verses.ar: إِنَّ مَعَ ٱلْعُسْرِ يُسْرًا
verses.en: Indeed, with hardship [will be] ease.

title: Emotional Intelligence
tag: IQ gets you hired. Emotional intelligence decides how far you lead.
source: Daniel Goleman, Emotional Intelligence (1995); 'What Makes a Leader', Harvard Business Review (1998); Goleman, Boyatzis and McKee, Primal Leadership (2002)
hadith: The strong man is not the one who wrestles others down. The strong man is the one who controls himself when he is angry.
Sahih al-Bukhari 6114, Sahih Muslim 2609
opening: In 1998 the Harvard Business Review published an article by the psychologist Daniel Goleman that became one of its most requested pieces ever. Its argument was that technical skill and intelligence are threshold requirements for leadership. What separates outstanding leaders from average ones is something else.
idea: Goleman identified five components of emotional intelligence. Self-awareness: knowing your own emotions, strengths, weaknesses and drives. Self-regulation: controlling disruptive impulses and moods, and thinking before acting. Motivation: a passion for the work beyond money or status. Empathy: considering others' feelings, especially when making decisions. And social skill: managing relationships and building networks. He reported that in the competency models of many organisations he analysed, these capacities became more important the higher a person rose. At senior levels, he reported that close to ninety percent of the difference between star performers and average ones came from emotional intelligence rather than cognitive ability.
mechanics: The deeper science is about the brain. Emotions arise quickly in the limbic system, faster than the reasoning parts of the brain can respond. Goleman popularised the term 'amygdala hijack' for moments when an emotional reaction overwhelms judgement: the angry email, the humiliating remark in a meeting. Self-regulation is the trained capacity to notice the surge and create a gap before acting. In Primal Leadership he added that a leader's mood is contagious. Teams literally catch the emotional state of their leader, so an anxious or irritable leader spreads anxiety and irritation through the whole organisation. Leadership, at its root, is emotional.
practice: Goleman also argued that emotional intelligence can be learned, but not through lectures. It requires practice, feedback and time, because it means retraining habits. Regulators, auditors and compliance officers face this daily: delivering unwelcome findings to senior people without triggering defensiveness, staying calm when challenged, reading the mood of a board. The leader who masters his own state can carry hard messages that others cannot.
faith: Allah praises those who spend in ease and hardship, who restrain anger, and who pardon people; and Allah loves those who do good. Ibn Kathir notes that restraining anger means not acting on it, and pardoning means going further and letting go of the grievance. The Prophet, peace be upon him, gave the most precise definition of self-regulation: true strength is controlling yourself in anger. He also gave practical steps: to seek refuge in Allah from Shaytan, to change your posture, and to stay silent. Fourteen centuries before neuroscience, the Sunnah taught the pause.
nigerian: The Igbo saying «Onye ajụjụ anaghị efu ụzọ», the one who asks questions does not lose his way, captures empathy in action. A leader who asks how others see a matter before pronouncing on it rarely loses his people.
practices: When you feel anger rising, say «A'udhu billahi min al-shaytan al-rajim», sit down, and wait before replying.
Before each important meeting, ask: what is my mood, and what will the room catch from me?
Once a week, ask a colleague how a decision of yours landed with the team, and just listen.
reflect: Which emotion most often hijacks my judgement?
What mood do my team catch from me on a normal day?
closing: The strong one is the one who controls himself. Master your own heart, and you will be able to lead others through theirs.

verses.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ يُنفِقُونَ فِى ٱلسَّرَّآءِ وَٱلضَّرَّآءِ وَٱلْكَٰظِمِينَ ٱلْغَيْظَ وَٱلْعَافِينَ عَنِ ٱلنَّاسِ وَٱللَّهُ يُحِبُّ ٱلْمُحْسِنِينَ
verses.en: Who spend [in the cause of Allāh] during ease and hardship and who restrain anger and who pardon the people - and Allāh loves the doers of good;

title: Psychological Safety
tag: Teams that admit more errors may be the ones making fewer.
source: Amy Edmondson, 'Psychological Safety and Learning Behavior in Work Teams' (1999); The Fearless Organization (2018); Right Kind of Wrong (2023)
opening: As a young researcher, Amy Edmondson studied hospital teams expecting to confirm that better teams make fewer medication errors. Her data showed the opposite: the better teams appeared to make more. The puzzle launched a career at Harvard Business School and a concept now used by organisations worldwide.
idea: The better teams were not making more mistakes. They were reporting more. In teams where people felt safe to speak up, errors were admitted, discussed and fixed. In teams led by fear, errors were hidden until they became disasters. Edmondson called this psychological safety: a shared belief that the team is safe for interpersonal risk-taking. It means people can ask a question, admit a mistake, raise a concern or offer a wild idea without fear of being humiliated or punished. It is not about being nice, and it is not about lowering standards. Google's large study of its own teams, Project Aristotle, later found psychological safety to be the most important factor in team effectiveness.
mechanics: Edmondson draws a two-by-two grid. Low safety and low standards produce apathy. High safety and low standards produce comfort. Low safety and high standards produce anxiety, where people work hard but hide problems. Only high safety combined with high standards produces a learning zone. She also distinguishes three kinds of failure: preventable failures in routine work, which should be minimised; complex failures, which arise from many small factors combining; and intelligent failures, small experiments in new territory, which should be welcomed because they produce learning. Leaders build safety by framing work as a learning problem, by acknowledging their own fallibility, by asking genuine questions, and by responding productively when someone brings bad news.
practice: Silence is the great risk in regulated institutions. Many corporate scandals were known to junior staff long before they became public. A compliance function only works when people tell the truth early. The leader's first reaction to bad news teaches the whole organisation whether bad news is welcome. Thank the messenger first, solve the problem second, and investigate causes without hunting for scapegoats.
faith: Allah describes the believers as those whose affairs are conducted by mutual consultation. Shura only works when people feel free to speak. Before the Battle of Badr, a companion, al-Hubab ibn al-Mundhir, asked the Prophet, peace be upon him, whether the camp's position was revelation or a matter of opinion and strategy. When told it was opinion, he proposed a better position near the wells, and the Prophet accepted it, as recorded in the sirah of Ibn Ishaq. The greatest leader of all created a team in which a companion could correct the plan.
nigerian: The Yoruba say «Àgbà kì í wà lọ́jà, kí orí ọmọ títún wọ́»: an elder does not sit in the market while a baby's head is twisted on its back. A leader's presence is supposed to make the vulnerable safe. And the Hausa say «Hannu ɗaya ba ya ɗaukar jinka»: one hand cannot lift a thatched roof.
practices: In your next meeting, ask: what am I missing? Then wait through the silence.
When someone reports a mistake, say thank you before anything else.
Share one mistake of your own with your team this month, and what you learned.
reflect: What is the last piece of bad news my team brought me early, and how did I respond?
Which quadrant is my team in: apathy, comfort, anxiety or learning?
closing: Consult, and make it safe to speak. A team that can tell its leader the truth can correct anything.

verses.ar: وَٱلَّذِينَ ٱسْتَجَابُوا۟ لِرَبِّهِمْ وَأَقَامُوا۟ ٱلصَّلَوٰةَ وَأَمْرُهُمْ شُورَىٰ بَيْنَهُمْ وَمِمَّا رَزَقْنَٰهُمْ يُنفِقُونَ
verses.en: And those who have responded to their Lord and established prayer and whose affair is [determined by] consultation among themselves, and from what We have provided them, they spend,

title: Leading Change
tag: Why most transformations fail, and the eight steps that make them stick.
source: John Kotter, 'Leading Change: Why Transformation Efforts Fail', Harvard Business Review (1995); Leading Change (1996)
opening: John Kotter studied more than a hundred companies attempting major change and concluded that most of them failed, or achieved far less than they hoped. His 1995 Harvard Business Review article explaining why remains one of the most cited pieces ever written on management.
idea: Kotter's insight was that change fails in predictable ways, at predictable stages. He proposed eight steps. Establish a sense of urgency. Form a powerful guiding coalition. Create a vision. Communicate the vision, far more than seems necessary. Empower others to act on it by removing obstacles. Plan for and create short-term wins. Consolidate improvements and produce still more change. And institutionalise new approaches in the culture. Skipping a step creates only the illusion of speed. The most common mistake, he found, is the very first: not establishing enough urgency, so people stay comfortable with the status quo.
mechanics: Each step addresses a specific failure. Without a guiding coalition of people with enough power, credibility and expertise, change is fought by the old structure. Without a clear vision that can be explained in five minutes, efforts dissolve into confusing projects. Undercommunicating by a factor of ten, Kotter said, is common: leaders send one memo and assume the message has landed. Without short-term wins within months, critics gain ground and believers grow tired. And declaring victory too soon is fatal, because new practices only stick when they are rooted in culture, in 'the way we do things here', and when the next generation of leaders embodies them.
practice: Kotter later added that organisations need a dual operating system: the normal hierarchy to run today's business, and a more agile network of volunteers to drive strategic change. For a strategy or accountability unit, this is practical. Change cannot be decreed by a memo from the top. It needs a coalition, a story people can repeat, quick visible wins, and patience to anchor it in culture.
faith: Has the time not come for those who believe that their hearts should become humble at the remembrance of Allah? This verse is a call to urgency. Al-Dhahabi records in Siyar A'lam al-Nubala' that al-Fudayl ibn 'Iyad, before his repentance, heard it recited at night and said: yes, my Lord, the time has come. His whole life turned on that moment. The Prophet's own method of change in Madinah followed a careful sequence: building a core of committed companions, a clear message repeated constantly, early wins, and gradual institutionalisation. Even the prohibition of alcohol came in stages, as 'A'ishah explained in Sahih al-Bukhari, because hearts had to be prepared first.
nigerian: The Hausa say «Zomo ba ya kamuwa a zaune»: you do not catch a hare by sitting down. Urgency and action belong together. But the Hausa also say «Sannu sannu bai hana zuwa», slowly does not stop you arriving: lasting change is staged, not rushed.
practices: Write your change vision in two sentences that a new staff member could repeat.
Name five people who must be in the guiding coalition, and meet each of them this month.
Plan one visible win within the next ninety days, and celebrate it publicly.
reflect: Which of Kotter's eight steps have I skipped in my current change effort?
Has the time not come for the change I keep postponing in myself?
closing: Change begins with urgency and ends in culture. Build the coalition, repeat the vision, win early, and do not declare victory too soon.

verses.ar: أَلَمْ يَأْنِ لِلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ أَن تَخْشَعَ قُلُوبُهُمْ لِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ وَمَا نَزَلَ مِنَ ٱلْحَقِّ وَلَا يَكُونُوا۟ كَٱلَّذِينَ أُوتُوا۟ ٱلْكِتَٰبَ مِن قَبْلُ فَطَالَ عَلَيْهِمُ ٱلْأَمَدُ فَقَسَتْ قُلُوبُهُمْ وَكَثِيرٌ مِّنْهُمْ فَٰسِقُونَ
verses.en: Has the time not come for those who have believed that their hearts should become humbly submissive at the remembrance of Allāh and what has come down of the truth? And let them not be like those who were given the Scripture before, and a long period passed over them, so their hearts hardened; and many of them are defiantly disobedient.

title: The Trust Triangle
tag: Trust rests on three legs: authenticity, logic and empathy.
source: Frances Frei and Anne Morriss, 'Begin with Trust', Harvard Business Review (2020); Unleashed (2020)
hadith: The signs of a hypocrite are three: when he speaks he lies, when he promises he breaks it, and when he is entrusted he betrays the trust.
Sahih al-Bukhari 33, Sahih Muslim 59
opening: Frances Frei, a professor at Harvard Business School, was called in to help repair trust at some of the world's best known companies after public crises. From that work she and Anne Morriss developed a simple model that explains why people trust us, and why they stop.
idea: People trust you when they experience three things. Authenticity: they believe they are dealing with the real you. Logic: they believe in your judgement and competence, that your reasoning is sound. And empathy: they believe you care about them and their success. When trust is lost, it is almost always because one of these three legs has wobbled. Frei and Morriss found that for most leaders one leg is the usual weak point. They call it your 'wobble'. For many high achievers, the most common wobble is empathy: they are so focused on the problem, so quick and so sure, that people feel unheard.
mechanics: Each wobble has a remedy. For logic, the issue is often not poor reasoning but poor communication. They suggest starting with the conclusion and then giving the supporting points, rather than walking listeners through the whole journey. For empathy, the remedy is attention: put down the phone, ask questions, and let others finish before you respond. For authenticity, the risk is hiding parts of yourself to fit in, which makes people sense something is held back. Frei argues that organisations should make it safe for people to bring their full selves to work, because when people hide, trust and performance both fall. Trust, in their framing, is the foundation that makes empowerment possible.
practice: Their larger argument is that leadership is about making other people better as a result of your presence, and making sure that impact continues in your absence. You cannot empower people who do not trust you, and you cannot trust people you have not invested in. For a compliance officer, whose work depends on others disclosing problems voluntarily, the trust triangle is the infrastructure of the whole function.
faith: Allah says: We offered the trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, and they declined to bear it and feared it, but man undertook it. Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn 'Abbas that the trust is the obligations of religion: everything a person is responsible for. Before revelation, the Quraysh called the Prophet, peace be upon him, al-Amin, the trustworthy, and even his enemies left their valuables with him. The hadith of the hypocrite names the three ways trust dies: lying, breaking promises, and betraying what you were entrusted with.
nigerian: The Igbo say «Ezi aha ka ego»: a good name is better than wealth. Ngozi Okonjo-Iweala's account of her years at Nigeria's finance ministry, Reforming the Unreformable, keeps returning to credibility with stakeholders as what made hard reforms possible. Credibility, once earned, buys time for difficult decisions.
practices: Ask two trusted colleagues which leg of the triangle is your wobble.
In your next three presentations, state the conclusion in the first sentence.
In one conversation a day, put the phone away and ask one more question than you normally would.
reflect: When did someone last stop trusting me, and which leg wobbled?
Do I keep every promise, even small ones, that I make at work and at home?
closing: Authenticity, logic and empathy. Guard all three, keep your promises, and carry your trust as the heavy amanah it is.

verses.ar: إِنَّا عَرَضْنَا ٱلْأَمَانَةَ عَلَى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَٱلْأَرْضِ وَٱلْجِبَالِ فَأَبَيْنَ أَن يَحْمِلْنَهَا وَأَشْفَقْنَ مِنْهَا وَحَمَلَهَا ٱلْإِنسَٰنُ إِنَّهُۥ كَانَ ظَلُومًا جَهُولًا
verses.en: Indeed, We offered the Trust to the heavens and the earth and the mountains, and they declined to bear it and feared it; but man [undertook to] bear it. Indeed, he was unjust and ignorant.

title: The Harvard Study of Adult Development
tag: The longest study of human life found one clear lesson: relationships.
source: Robert Waldinger and Marc Schulz, The Good Life (2023); George Vaillant, Triumphs of Experience (2012)
opening: In 1938, researchers at Harvard began following 268 young men, sophomores at the university, through their entire lives. A parallel study followed several hundred boys from poor neighbourhoods of Boston. Later their wives and children joined. It is one of the longest studies of adult life ever conducted, and it is still running.
idea: Over more than eight decades, the researchers measured health, careers, income, marriages, habits and happiness, through questionnaires, interviews, medical records and even brain scans. The current director, the psychiatrist Robert Waldinger, summarises the clearest finding: good relationships keep us happier and healthier. The people who were most satisfied in their relationships at age fifty were the healthiest at age eighty. Close relationships predicted long and happy lives better than social class, IQ, or even genes. Loneliness, by contrast, proved as damaging to health as smoking or heavy drinking.
mechanics: The study's earlier director, George Vaillant, found that it was not the number of friends that mattered, but the quality of close relationships. People in warm, secure relationships had sharper memories into old age. Waldinger and his co-director Marc Schulz describe 'social fitness': relationships, like muscles, weaken without exercise. They need regular attention, curiosity and small acts of care. Conflict itself was not the danger; couples who bickered but felt they could count on each other did well. The danger was neglect, drifting into isolation as work, ambition and screens consumed the time that relationships need.
practice: Many of the men in the study, near the end of their lives, said the same thing: they wished they had spent less time working and more time with the people they loved. For a professional carrying multiple demanding roles and living apart from family much of the time, the finding is a direct challenge. Relationships at a distance survive only through deliberate, regular investment.
faith: Worship Allah and associate nothing with Him, and to parents do good, and to relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbour, the neighbour farther away, the companion at your side, the traveller, and those your right hands possess. Allah does not like the arrogant and boastful. This verse sets out a full map of social fitness, a series of widening circles of care, each one an act of worship. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that Jibril kept advising him about the neighbour until he thought the neighbour would be made an heir, as recorded in both Sahihs. Islam made relationships a pillar of the good life fourteen centuries before Harvard confirmed it.
nigerian: The Hausa say «Kowa ya bar gida, gida ya bar shi»: whoever leaves home, home leaves him. Distance and success can quietly separate us from the people who matter most. Nigerian traditions of visiting, greeting and family gatherings are not burdens on a busy life; they are its foundation.
practices: Schedule a weekly call with each of your children, and ask about their world, not only their results.
Reconnect with one old friend this month.
Do one small act of care for a neighbour or colleague without being asked.
reflect: Which relationship have I been neglecting because of work?
At eighty, what will I wish I had done more of?
closing: Worship Allah, and do good to the circles He placed around you. The good life is built from relationships, tended with care.

verses.ar: وَٱعْبُدُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَلَا تُشْرِكُوا۟ بِهِۦ شَيْـًٔا وَبِٱلْوَٰلِدَيْنِ إِحْسَٰنًا وَبِذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ وَٱلْيَتَٰمَىٰ وَٱلْمَسَٰكِينِ وَٱلْجَارِ ذِى ٱلْقُرْبَىٰ وَٱلْجَارِ ٱلْجُنُبِ وَٱلصَّاحِبِ بِٱلْجَنۢبِ وَٱبْنِ ٱلسَّبِيلِ وَمَا مَلَكَتْ أَيْمَٰنُكُمْ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُحِبُّ مَن كَانَ مُخْتَالًا فَخُورًا
verses.en: Worship Allāh and associate nothing with Him, and to parents do good, and to relatives, orphans, the needy, the near neighbor, the neighbor farther away, the companion at your side, the traveler, and those whom your right hands possess. Indeed, Allāh does not like those who are self-deluding and boastful,

title: Managing Oneself
tag: Know your strengths, how you work, what you value, and where you belong.
source: Peter Drucker, 'Managing Oneself', Harvard Business Review (1999); The Effective Executive (1967)
opening: In 1999, at the age of eighty-nine, Peter Drucker wrote a short article for the Harvard Business Review that many consider his most important gift to individuals. In an age of knowledge work, he argued, people will outlive their organisations and must learn to manage their own careers.
idea: Drucker asks a series of questions. What are my strengths? Most people think they know, and most are wrong. How do I perform? Am I a reader or a listener? Do I learn by writing, by talking, or by doing? Do I work best alone or with others, as a decision maker or an adviser? What are my values? If your values conflict with your organisation's, you will be frustrated and ineffective, however capable you are. Where do I belong? And what should I contribute? Excellence, he said, comes from building on strengths, not fixing weaknesses. It takes far more energy to improve from incompetence to mediocrity than from good performance to excellence.
mechanics: The tool for discovering strengths is feedback analysis. Whenever you make a key decision or take a key action, write down what you expect to happen. Nine or twelve months later, compare the actual results with your expectations. Drucker said he had practised this for decades, and that within two or three years it reveals where your strengths lie, what you are doing that prevents you from benefiting from them, and where you have no strengths at all. He traced the method to a fourteenth-century German theologian and to John Calvin and Ignatius of Loyola, who built similar practices into their communities. Drucker also wrote about relationships: take responsibility for communication, learn how your colleagues work and adapt to them, and plan for the second half of your life, through a parallel career or a non-profit venture, because most people outgrow a single career.
practice: For someone holding several leadership roles at once, Drucker's questions are a filter. Which of these roles uses my real strengths? Where am I spending energy on things I do poorly that someone else could do well? Is there a role where my values and the organisation's values pull against each other? The answers guide what to delegate, what to decline, and where to invest.
faith: Say: each works according to his manner, and your Lord is most knowing of who is best guided in way. The word shakilah, translated 'manner', was explained by the early mufassirun as a person's nature, disposition and way. Allah created people with different natures and gifts. The Prophet, peace be upon him, recognised and deployed his companions' strengths: Khalid ibn al-Walid in command, Zayd ibn Thabit in writing the revelation, Abu 'Ubaydah as the trustworthy one of the ummah, Bilal for the call to prayer. Managing oneself begins with knowing how Allah made you.
nigerian: Too many talented Nigerians spend careers in roles chosen by family pressure or prestige, not by strength or calling. Drucker's questions give permission to ask, respectfully, where one's gifts can do the most good, for oneself, one's family and the country.
practices: Start a feedback analysis: for your next three key decisions, write down what you expect, and set a date to review.
Answer Drucker's question in writing: am I a reader or a listener?
List your roles and mark each: uses my strength, neutral, or drains me.
reflect: Where am I working against my own nature?
Do my values truly match the organisations I serve?
closing: Each works according to his manner. Know how Allah made you, build on your strengths, and contribute where you belong.

verses.ar: قُلْ كُلٌّ يَعْمَلُ عَلَىٰ شَاكِلَتِهِۦ فَرَبُّكُمْ أَعْلَمُ بِمَنْ هُوَ أَهْدَىٰ سَبِيلًا
verses.en: Say, "Each works according to his manner, but your Lord is most knowing of who is best guided in way."

title: Manage Your Energy, Not Your Time
tag: Time is finite. Energy can be renewed.
source: Tony Schwartz and Catherine McCarthy, 'Manage Your Energy, Not Your Time', Harvard Business Review (2007); Jim Loehr and Tony Schwartz, The Power of Full Engagement (2003)
opening: In 2007, Tony Schwartz and Catherine McCarthy of The Energy Project published an article in the Harvard Business Review based on work with executives at major banks and companies. Its title captured a shift many leaders needed.
idea: Most organisations respond to rising demands by asking people to work longer hours. But time is finite, and long hours eventually lead to exhaustion, disengagement and mistakes. Energy, unlike time, can be systematically expanded and regularly renewed. The authors describe four sources of energy. Physical: the body, through sleep, nutrition, exercise and rest. Emotional: the quality of our feelings, positive emotions fuel performance while anxiety and anger drain it. Mental: the ability to focus, without constant distraction. And spiritual: a sense of meaning and purpose in what we do. Performance depends on managing all four.
mechanics: The central insight, drawn from sports science, is that humans are designed to oscillate between spending energy and recovering it. Athletes improve by alternating stress and rest; constant effort without recovery leads to breakdown. The authors recommend rituals: specific behaviours done at fixed times until they become automatic, so they do not depend on willpower. Examples include stepping away from the desk every ninety minutes, getting adequate sleep, doing the most important task first thing in the morning before email, practising deep breathing in tense moments, expressing appreciation to others, and identifying the activities that give you the deepest sense of meaning. In their pilot programme at a large bank, participants reported better results and greater wellbeing than a comparison group.
practice: Multitasking is a key drain. Each switch between tasks costs time and attention. Leaders who protect blocks of uninterrupted focus, recover deliberately, and connect their work to a deeper purpose sustain high performance over decades rather than burning out in years.
faith: And We made your sleep a means of rest, and made the night as clothing, and made the day for livelihood. Allah built oscillation into creation: night and day, rest and work. And He built rituals into the believer's day: five prayers spread from dawn to night, each one a pause that renews the four energies at once. The body moves, the emotions settle, the mind focuses, and the spirit reconnects to its purpose. The Prophet, peace be upon him, used to say to Bilal: give us rest with it, O Bilal, meaning the call to prayer, in a hadith recorded by Abu Dawud. Prayer was his renewal, not his burden.
nigerian: Nigerian professionals often face long commutes, irregular power supply and heavy family obligations on top of demanding jobs. Energy management is not a luxury here; it is survival. Fixed rituals, protected sleep and prayer used as true rest rather than a hurried interruption can be the difference between sustained performance and burnout.
practices: Use each of the five prayers as a real reset: arrive a few minutes early, breathe, and leave the work behind.
Do your most important task for the first ninety minutes of the workday, before email.
Fix a consistent bedtime for the next two weeks.
reflect: Which of my four energies is most depleted right now?
Do I treat prayer as a burden in my schedule, or as my rest?
closing: Your time is fixed, but your energy can be renewed. Rest at night, work in the day, and let the prayer be your rest, as it was for the Prophet.

verses.ar: وَجَعَلْنَا نَوْمَكُمْ سُبَاتًا
verses.en: And made your sleep [a means for] rest

verses.ar: وَجَعَلْنَا ٱلَّيْلَ لِبَاسًا
verses.en: And made the night as clothing

verses.ar: وَجَعَلْنَا ٱلنَّهَارَ مَعَاشًا
verses.en: And made the day for livelihood

title: How Will You Measure Your Life?
tag: Business theory turned on the questions that matter most.
source: Clayton Christensen, 'How Will You Measure Your Life?', Harvard Business Review (2010); How Will You Measure Your Life? (2012, with James Allworth and Karen Dillon)
opening: At the end of his course at Harvard Business School, Clayton Christensen would ask his students to apply everything they had learned about strategy to their own lives. In 2010, recovering from cancer, he shared his answers in a Harvard Business Review article that became one of the most widely read it ever published.
idea: Christensen asked his students three questions: How can I be sure that I will be happy in my career? How can I be sure that my relationships with my spouse and family become an enduring source of happiness? And how can I be sure I will stay out of jail? The last was not a joke. Several of his classmates had achieved great success, and some had ended up in unhappy marriages, estranged from their children, or in prison, as one did after the Enron collapse. None of them had planned that. They had made a series of small decisions that added up to a life they never intended.
mechanics: Christensen applied business theory. Resource allocation: a strategy is not what you say; it is where you spend your time, energy and money. High achievers instinctively allocate resources to activities that yield the most immediate, visible accomplishments, such as closing a deal or getting a promotion, and starve the things that pay off slowly, like family relationships, which show no measurable return until it is too late. Marginal cost thinking: companies make bad decisions by looking only at the marginal cost of doing something once. People do the same: 'just this once' I will cross this line. He wrote that it is easier to hold to your principles one hundred percent of the time than ninety-eight percent of the time, because the boundary, once crossed, is crossed again. He himself had decided never to play basketball on Sunday, even in a championship, and never regretted it.
practice: His final advice was about measurement. Do not worry about the level of individual prominence you achieve. Worry about the individuals you have helped become better people. He said he had come to understand that God does not have accountants and statisticians; He measures a life one person at a time.
faith: Competition in increase diverts you, until you visit the graveyards. Ibn Kathir explains that people are distracted from the Hereafter by competing in wealth, children and status, until death overtakes them. Christensen's resource allocation problem is exactly this: the visible rewards of competition steal the hours meant for what endures. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said that the son of Adam says, my wealth, my wealth; but what is yours of your wealth except what you ate and consumed, what you wore and wore out, or what you gave in charity and sent ahead? This is in Sahih Muslim. The measure of a life is what you send ahead.
nigerian: Nigerian society often measures success by visible markers: cars, houses, titles, the size of one's entourage. Christensen's questions, and the Qur'an's warning, invite a different measurement: the people you have raised, mentored and served, and the principles you kept when no one was watching.
practices: Track for one week where your hours actually go, and compare it with what you say matters most.
Name one principle you will keep one hundred percent of the time, with no 'just this once'.
Write the names of five people you want to help become better, starting with your own family.
reflect: Is my resource allocation matching my stated priorities?
What line have I crossed 'just this once' that could become a pattern?
closing: Do not let competition in increase divert you. Measure your life by the people you help become better, and by what you send ahead.

verses.ar: أَلْهَىٰكُمُ ٱلتَّكَاثُرُ
verses.en: Competition in [worldly] increase diverts you

verses.ar: حَتَّىٰ زُرْتُمُ ٱلْمَقَابِرَ
verses.en: Until you visit the graveyards.

title: Immunity to Change
tag: Why we don't change, even when we truly want to.
source: Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey, 'The Real Reason People Won't Change', Harvard Business Review (2001); Immunity to Change (2009)
opening: Robert Kegan and Lisa Lahey, developmental psychologists at the Harvard Graduate School of Education, studied a puzzle familiar to everyone. People sincerely commit to change, delegate more, listen better, lose weight, stop procrastinating, and then fail, again and again. Their explanation is not weak willpower.
idea: Kegan and Lahey argue that we each have an immune system for change. It is not a weakness but a protective mechanism, quietly working to keep us safe from something we fear. Alongside our stated commitment, say, to delegate more, we hold a hidden competing commitment, such as to never be associated with a failure, or to always be seen as the one who knows. The competing commitment is perfectly rational in its own terms, and it is stronger than our stated goal. So we have one foot on the gas and one on the brake. Pressing harder on the gas, through more effort or resolutions, only burns out the engine.
mechanics: Their method maps the immunity in four columns. Column one: my improvement goal. Column two: what I am doing or not doing instead, honestly listed. Column three: my hidden competing commitments, found by asking what fear would arise if I did the opposite of column two. Column four: the big assumptions that make those commitments seem necessary, such as 'if I delegate and something goes wrong, people will think I am incompetent and I will lose my position'. Big assumptions are held as truth, but they are often untested. The way forward is not to fight the behaviour, but to design small, safe experiments that test the assumption, and to observe what actually happens. Gradually the assumption loosens, and the change becomes possible.
practice: Kegan and Lahey also describe stages of adult mental development: the socialised mind, shaped by the expectations of others; the self-authoring mind, guided by its own internal compass; and the self-transforming mind, able to hold multiple perspectives and question its own framework. The demands of modern leadership increasingly require the higher stages, and working through one's immunities is how adults grow from one stage to the next.
faith: Indeed, Allah will not change the condition of a people until they change what is within themselves. The change Allah asks for begins inside, in the beliefs and fears that drive behaviour. Ibn al-Qayyim, in al-Fawa'id, described how deeds grow from thoughts, which become desires, which become resolutions and then actions. To change the action you must reach the thought. The Qur'an also names the deepest competing commitments: fear of poverty, fear of people's opinion, love of praise. Shaytan promises you poverty, says Allah in Surah al-Baqarah. Many of our big assumptions are whispers that have never been tested against tawakkul.
nigerian: Achebe described how the Igbo say that when a person says yes, his chi also says yes: «Onye kwe, chi ya ekwe». The individual's will is part of the change. But Kegan would add that you must first uncover the hidden 'no' inside that resists your 'yes'.
practices: Fill in the four columns for one change you have failed to make.
Design one small, safe experiment this week to test your big assumption.
Before acting, ask: what am I afraid would happen if I did the opposite?
reflect: What hidden commitment protects me from a fear I rarely admit?
Which of my big assumptions is really a whisper I have never tested?
closing: Change begins within. Find the hidden brake, test the assumption behind it, and let Allah change what you are willing to change in yourself.

verses.ar: لَهُۥ مُعَقِّبَٰتٌ مِّنۢ بَيْنِ يَدَيْهِ وَمِنْ خَلْفِهِۦ يَحْفَظُونَهُۥ مِنْ أَمْرِ ٱللَّهِ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ لَا يُغَيِّرُ مَا بِقَوْمٍ حَتَّىٰ يُغَيِّرُوا۟ مَا بِأَنفُسِهِمْ وَإِذَآ أَرَادَ ٱللَّهُ بِقَوْمٍ سُوٓءًا فَلَا مَرَدَّ لَهُۥ وَمَا لَهُم مِّن دُونِهِۦ مِن وَالٍ
verses.en: For him [i.e., each one] are successive [angels] before and behind him who protect him by the decree of Allāh. Indeed, Allāh will not change the condition of a people until they change what is in themselves. And when Allāh intends for a people ill, there is no repelling it. And there is not for them besides Him any patron.

title: From Strength to Strength
sub: Arthur Brooks · Harvard Kennedy School & HBS
tag: Success at fifty requires a different kind of intelligence than success at thirty.
source: Arthur C. Brooks, From Strength to Strength (2022); Brooks and Oprah Winfrey, Build the Life You Want (2023); 'How to Build a Life' column, The Atlantic
opening: Arthur Brooks was a professional musician, then an economist, then the president of a major Washington think tank, and is now a professor at Harvard who teaches one of its most popular courses, on the science of happiness. On a flight, he overheard an elderly man telling his wife that he wished he were dead, because nobody cared about him anymore. Later, Brooks recognised him as a man who had once been famous. The encounter changed his research.
idea: Brooks draws on the psychologist Raymond Cattell's distinction between two kinds of intelligence. Fluid intelligence is the ability to reason quickly, solve new problems and innovate. It peaks in early adulthood and declines from our late thirties and forties. Crystallised intelligence is the ability to use accumulated knowledge and wisdom: to see patterns, teach, mentor and synthesise. It rises through the forties, fifties and sixties. Many high achievers suffer in midlife because they cling to the fluid curve, trying to keep winning in the way they did at thirty. The secret is to jump to the second curve: to move from innovator to teacher, from solo performer to mentor, from striving to wisdom.
mechanics: Brooks also defines happiness with three 'macronutrients': enjoyment, which is pleasure combined with connection and memory; satisfaction, the joy of reward after effort; and meaning, a sense of coherence, purpose and significance. He warns that satisfaction is fleeting by design, which is why achievement addiction leaves people perpetually hungry. His prescriptions are old ones: cultivate deep relationships, practise gratitude, serve others, develop a faith or philosophy of life, and practise what he calls 'subtraction': removing attachments to money, power, pleasure and fame. He uses a striking image from Hindu teaching about the stages of life, and from the Christian tradition: in the second half of life, the task is to give away what you have learned.
practice: For a leader approaching or in midlife, the practical question is: which parts of my work should shift from doing to teaching? Writing down methods, mentoring younger staff, building institutions that outlast you. The crystallised intelligence curve rewards those who share what they know.
faith: Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allah. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allah hearts are assured. Brooks found that achievement alone cannot satisfy the heart. The Qur'an names what does. Ibn al-Qayyim taught, in a passage often quoted from his works, that the heart has a need that nothing can fill except turning to Allah. And the Islamic tradition honours crystallised intelligence. The Prophet, peace be upon him, received revelation at forty, and the Qur'an mentions the age of forty as the age of full maturity in Surah al-Ahqaf. The scholars' greatest works were often written late in life, when knowledge had matured into wisdom.
nigerian: The Hausa proverb says «Abin da babba ya hango yana kwance, yaro ko ya hau rimi ba zai gani ba»: what an elder sees while lying down, a child cannot see even from the top of a silk-cotton tree. This is crystallised intelligence. Nigerian culture has always honoured the elder's wisdom; Brooks shows why, and how to grow into it.
practices: Identify one skill or method you can teach to a younger colleague this month.
Practise one act of subtraction: give up one attachment to status, possession or praise.
Each morning, spend five minutes in dhikr before reaching for your phone.
reflect: Am I clinging to the first curve, or preparing for the second?
Which of my three happiness nutrients is missing: enjoyment, satisfaction or meaning?
closing: Achievement fades, but wisdom grows. Move from strength to strength, teach what you know, and let your heart find rest in the remembrance of Allah.

verses.ar: ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَتَطْمَئِنُّ قُلُوبُهُم بِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ أَلَا بِذِكْرِ ٱللَّهِ تَطْمَئِنُّ ٱلْقُلُوبُ
verses.en: Those who have believed and whose hearts are assured by the remembrance of Allāh. Unquestionably, by the remembrance of Allāh hearts are assured."

title: What Is Strategy?
tag: Strategy is choosing what not to do.
source: Michael Porter, Competitive Strategy (1980); 'What Is Strategy?', Harvard Business Review (1996); 'The Five Competitive Forces That Shape Strategy', HBR (2008)
opening: Michael Porter is among the most cited scholars in business history. From Harvard Business School he gave managers two tools that are still taught everywhere: the five forces that shape an industry, and a definition of strategy that most organisations still fail to live by.
idea: Porter's 1996 article made a sharp distinction. Operational effectiveness means doing the same things as your rivals, but better: faster, cheaper, with fewer errors. It is necessary, but it is not strategy, because best practices are quickly copied and everyone converges. Strategy means deliberately choosing a different set of activities to deliver a unique mix of value. It requires trade-offs: choosing what not to do, which customers not to serve, and which needs not to meet. A company that tries to be everything to everyone has no strategy. And the activities must fit together and reinforce each other, so that the whole system is hard to copy even if each part is visible.
mechanics: To understand where profit can be made, Porter identified five forces that shape every industry: the rivalry among existing competitors, the threat of new entrants, the bargaining power of buyers, the bargaining power of suppliers, and the threat of substitute products or services. An industry's profitability depends on the collective strength of these forces, not on how glamorous or fast-growing it is. He also described generic positions, competing on lower cost or on differentiation, either broadly or in a focused niche, and warned against being 'stuck in the middle'. His value chain shows that competitive advantage lives in the specific activities a firm performs, from inbound logistics to after-sales service.
practice: For a Nigerian fund manager, the five forces are a practical map. Buyers, meaning investors, have growing power as alternatives multiply. Substitutes include fintech savings apps and real estate. New entrants face regulatory barriers, which is a protection. And a distinctive position, such as Shariah-compliant investing with credible screening and governance, creates trade-offs that conventional competitors cannot easily copy without changing what they are. The hard discipline is saying no to opportunities that do not fit.
faith: O you who believe, fear Allah, and let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow. Ibn Kathir explains it as a call to take account of yourself before you are taken to account, and to look at what you have stored up for the Day of Return. This is the ultimate strategic question: what am I building for tomorrow? A believer's life also requires trade-offs. Time spent on one thing is not spent on another. Yusuf's plan for Egypt was a clear strategic choice: store in abundance, consume little, and accept the trade-off for the sake of survival.
nigerian: Aliko Dangote's group moved from trading imported cement to manufacturing it locally, a deliberate set of choices about where to compete and which activities to own. Whatever one thinks of the group, the lesson is Porter's: advantage comes from a system of activities that fit together, not from one clever move.
practices: Write your unit's or company's strategy in one sentence that includes what you will not do.
Map the five forces for one business you are responsible for.
Identify one opportunity you should decline because it does not fit.
reflect: Am I confusing working harder with having a strategy?
What have I put forth for tomorrow, in this life and the next?
closing: Strategy is the courage to choose, and the discipline to say no. Look to what you are putting forth for tomorrow.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ ٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ وَلْتَنظُرْ نَفْسٌ مَّا قَدَّمَتْ لِغَدٍ وَٱتَّقُوا۟ ٱللَّهَ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ خَبِيرٌۢ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ
verses.en: O you who have believed, fear Allāh. And let every soul look to what it has put forth for tomorrow - and fear Allāh. Indeed, Allāh is Aware of what you do.

title: Blue Ocean Strategy
sub: W. Chan Kim & Renée Mauborgne · INSEAD
tag: Instead of beating the competition, make it irrelevant.
source: W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, 'Blue Ocean Strategy', Harvard Business Review (2004); Blue Ocean Strategy (2005); Blue Ocean Shift (2017)
opening: Two professors at INSEAD, W. Chan Kim and Renée Mauborgne, studied strategic moves across more than a hundred years and thirty industries. They noticed that the most profitable moves did not come from defeating rivals. They came from escaping them.
idea: They describe two kinds of market space. Red oceans are existing industries, where boundaries are known and companies fight over the same customers until the water is red with competition and profits shrink. Blue oceans are new market spaces, created by offering something that breaks the usual trade-off between value and cost. The key is value innovation: simultaneously raising value for buyers and lowering cost, by rethinking which factors the industry competes on. Their famous example is Cirque du Soleil, which dropped expensive circus elements like animal acts and star performers, and added theatre, music and artistic storylines, attracting adults willing to pay theatre prices.
mechanics: The main tool is the four actions framework, often called the ERRC grid. Eliminate: which factors that the industry takes for granted should be removed entirely? Reduce: which should be reduced well below the industry standard? Raise: which should be raised well above it? Create: which should be created that the industry has never offered? The results are drawn on a strategy canvas, a simple chart comparing your offer to competitors across the key factors. They also urge looking at non-customers: people who use alternatives or do nothing at all, because the largest blue oceans are often found among those the industry has ignored.
practice: Blue ocean thinking is valuable in markets that look saturated. Ethical and Shariah-compliant investment in Nigeria, for example, has historically served a narrow audience. The non-customers, millions of people who avoid conventional finance on principle, are a potential blue ocean if the offer is designed for them: simple products, transparent screening, accessible minimums, and education in local languages. Eliminate jargon, reduce minimum investment, raise trust, create community.
faith: It is He who made the earth tame for you, so walk among its slopes and eat of His provision, and to Him is the resurrection. Allah's earth is wide, and His provision is not limited to one crowded market. The companions who migrated to Madinah, many of them traders, built a new market rather than competing in the existing one dominated by others. The Prophet, peace be upon him, and the companions established a market in Madinah free of the usual levies, according to a report in Sunan Ibn Majah, though scholars differ on its chain. Creating new value while removing unjust costs is an old Islamic principle.
nigerian: Nollywood is one of the world's great blue oceans. In the early 1990s, producers such as those behind Living in Bondage skipped cinemas and expensive film stock, shot quickly on video, and sold directly to homes. They eliminated what the film industry took for granted and created an audience of millions that Hollywood had never served.
practices: Draw an ERRC grid for one service you offer: one item each to eliminate, reduce, raise and create.
List three groups of non-customers for your organisation and why they stay away.
Sketch a strategy canvas comparing your offer to two competitors.
reflect: Am I fighting in a red ocean out of habit?
Who is my organisation ignoring that it could serve?
closing: Do not only fight for a share of the crowded market. Allah's earth is wide. Create new value, and make the competition irrelevant.

verses.ar: هُوَ ٱلَّذِى جَعَلَ لَكُمُ ٱلْأَرْضَ ذَلُولًا فَٱمْشُوا۟ فِى مَنَاكِبِهَا وَكُلُوا۟ مِن رِّزْقِهِۦ وَإِلَيْهِ ٱلنُّشُورُ
verses.en: It is He who made the earth tame for you - so walk among its slopes and eat of His provision - and to Him is the resurrection.

title: Disruptive Innovation
tag: Why great, well-managed companies are overtaken by simpler, cheaper rivals.
source: Clayton Christensen, The Innovator's Dilemma (1997); Christensen, Raynor and McDonald, 'What Is Disruptive Innovation?', Harvard Business Review (2015); Competing Against Luck (2016)
opening: Clayton Christensen, a Harvard Business School professor and devout man of faith, asked a puzzling question: why do excellent companies, doing everything their management textbooks recommend, still fail? His answer became one of the most influential business ideas of the past thirty years.
idea: Christensen distinguished two kinds of innovation. Sustaining innovation makes good products better for existing, demanding customers. Leading firms are very good at it. Disruptive innovation starts with something simpler, cheaper and initially worse, aimed at customers the leaders ignore, either the low end of the market or people who previously could not afford or access the product at all. Leaders rationally ignore it, because it serves unprofitable customers and their best customers do not want it. Then the disruptor improves, moves upmarket, and eventually takes the mainstream. The dilemma is that the very practices that make a company great, listening to its best customers and investing in its highest margins, blind it to disruption.
mechanics: Christensen's later work added the theory of jobs to be done. Customers do not buy products; they 'hire' them to do a job in their lives. His team's famous example involved milkshakes bought early in the morning by commuters, who were hiring them to make a long, boring drive more bearable and keep them full until lunch. Understanding the job reveals real competitors and real opportunities. He also showed that disruption depends on a business model, not just a technology: the disruptor's costs and processes allow it to profit from customers the incumbent cannot serve profitably. Established firms that responded successfully often created separate units, free from the parent's priorities.
practice: Financial services is one of the most disrupted industries in Africa. Agent banking, mobile wallets and payment start-ups reached millions of people the banks found unprofitable. For established institutions, Christensen's lesson is uncomfortable: the threat is rarely the competitor that looks like you. It is the one serving customers you consider not worth your time.
faith: Such days of varying fortune We rotate among people. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah alternates victory and defeat, ease and hardship, among people and nations, so that the believers are tested and purified. No position is permanent. The companies that dominate today will not dominate forever, and the humble beginning of a disruptor resembles many stories of the Qur'an and the sirah: what the powerful dismiss as weak and insignificant often carries the future.
nigerian: Paystack, founded in Lagos in 2015 to make online payments simpler for small businesses, was acquired by Stripe in 2020. Point-of-sale agents in markets and villages now do jobs that bank branches never reached. Disruption in Nigeria has come from serving the overlooked.
practices: Ask: which customers does my organisation consider not worth serving? Who might serve them instead?
Describe the 'job' your main service is hired to do, in the customer's words.
Identify one simpler, cheaper alternative to your offer that you have been dismissing.
reflect: What am I dismissing today that may define tomorrow?
Am I too comfortable with the customers I already have?
closing: No position is permanent; Allah rotates the days among people. Watch the overlooked, understand the job, and keep learning.

verses.ar: إِن يَمْسَسْكُمْ قَرْحٌ فَقَدْ مَسَّ ٱلْقَوْمَ قَرْحٌ مِّثْلُهُۥ وَتِلْكَ ٱلْأَيَّامُ نُدَاوِلُهَا بَيْنَ ٱلنَّاسِ وَلِيَعْلَمَ ٱللَّهُ ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ وَيَتَّخِذَ مِنكُمْ شُهَدَآءَ وَٱللَّهُ لَا يُحِبُّ ٱلظَّٰلِمِينَ
verses.en: If a wound should touch you - there has already touched the [opposing] people a wound similar to it. And these days [of varying conditions] We alternate among the people so that Allāh may make evident those who believe and [may] take to Himself from among you martyrs - and Allāh does not like the wrongdoers -

title: Good Strategy, Bad Strategy
tag: Goals are not strategy. A strategy is a coherent response to a diagnosed challenge.
source: Richard Rumelt, Good Strategy Bad Strategy (2011); The Crux (2022)
opening: Richard Rumelt, a strategy professor at UCLA, spent decades advising corporations and governments. He grew frustrated at how many 'strategies' he read were nothing of the kind: lists of ambitions, slogans and budgets dressed up in confident language.
idea: Rumelt identifies the hallmarks of bad strategy. Fluff: impressive-sounding jargon that hides the absence of thinking. Failure to face the challenge: if you cannot name the problem, you cannot solve it. Mistaking goals for strategy: 'we will grow revenue by twenty percent' is a wish, not a plan. And bad strategic objectives: long lists of things to do, with no priorities and no explanation of how they overcome the obstacle. Good strategy, in contrast, has a simple core he calls the kernel, with three parts: a diagnosis, a guiding policy, and coherent actions.
mechanics: The diagnosis names and simplifies the critical challenge, explaining what is really going on. The guiding policy is the overall approach chosen to deal with that challenge, which rules out many other possible actions. Coherent actions are coordinated steps that carry out the policy, each reinforcing the others. Rumelt stresses that good strategy concentrates resources on a pivotal point where effort will produce the biggest result, instead of spreading them evenly to keep everyone happy. In his later book, The Crux, he argues that the strategist's real skill is finding the crux: the part of the problem that is both critical and solvable.
practice: For a strategy and accountability unit, Rumelt is a test to apply to every plan. Does it begin with a clear diagnosis that a skeptic would accept? Does the guiding policy rule anything out? Do the actions fit together, or are they a wish list from every department? A two-page strategy with a sharp diagnosis is worth more than a fifty-page document of goals.
faith: Yusuf said: you will plant for seven years consecutively, and what you harvest, leave in its spikes, except a little from which you will eat. Then will come after that seven difficult years which will consume what you saved. Then will come a year in which people will be given rain. This is the kernel in the Qur'an. The diagnosis: the king's dream, interpreted as seven years of plenty followed by seven of famine. The guiding policy: store the surplus. The coherent actions: plant consistently, store grain in the ear to preserve it, consume little, and distribute during famine. The scholars of tafsir note that keeping the grain in its spikes protects it from rot, a precise operational detail inside a strategic vision.
nigerian: Many Nigerian development plans have been strong on ambition and weak on diagnosis. The lesson from Rumelt and from Yusuf is the same: begin by naming the real problem honestly, then concentrate scarce resources on the point where they will make the most difference.
practices: Rewrite one current plan as a kernel: diagnosis, guiding policy, and three coherent actions.
Cross out every item in your plan that is a goal, not an action.
Identify the crux: the part of your challenge that is both critical and solvable.
reflect: Can I state the real problem in two sentences?
Is my strategy concentrating resources, or spreading them to keep everyone happy?
closing: Diagnose honestly, choose a guiding policy, and act coherently, as Yusuf did for Egypt. Goals are hopes; strategy is a plan to overcome the obstacle.

verses.ar: قَالَ تَزْرَعُونَ سَبْعَ سِنِينَ دَأَبًا فَمَا حَصَدتُّمْ فَذَرُوهُ فِى سُنۢبُلِهِۦٓ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِّمَّا تَأْكُلُونَ
verses.en: [Joseph] said, "You will plant for seven years consecutively; and what you harvest leave in its spikes, except a little from which you will eat.

verses.ar: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ سَبْعٌ شِدَادٌ يَأْكُلْنَ مَا قَدَّمْتُمْ لَهُنَّ إِلَّا قَلِيلًا مِّمَّا تُحْصِنُونَ
verses.en: Then will come after that seven difficult [years] which will consume what you advanced [i.e., saved] for them, except a little from which you will store.

verses.ar: ثُمَّ يَأْتِى مِنۢ بَعْدِ ذَٰلِكَ عَامٌ فِيهِ يُغَاثُ ٱلنَّاسُ وَفِيهِ يَعْصِرُونَ
verses.en: Then will come after that a year in which the people will be given rain and in which they will press [olives and grapes]."

title: The Four Disciplines of Execution
tag: Strategy fails in the whirlwind of daily work. Here is how to protect it.
