source: Chris McChesney, Sean Covey and Jim Huling, The 4 Disciplines of Execution (2012); Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan, Execution (2002)
opening: Larry Bossidy and Ram Charan wrote that execution is the great unaddressed issue in business: most strategies fail not because they are poor, but because they are not carried out. The team behind the Four Disciplines of Execution studied why, across thousands of teams, and found the enemy has a name.
idea: They call it the whirlwind: the urgent daily work needed to keep the operation running. Emails, crises, reports, meetings, requests from the boss. The whirlwind is necessary, and it consumes almost all available energy. New strategic goals, which require people to change behaviour, are constantly swallowed by it. The four disciplines are designed to carve out a small, protected space for what matters most. Discipline one: focus on the wildly important, one or two goals at most, each stated as 'from X to Y by when'. The more goals you have, they argue, the fewer you achieve.
mechanics: Discipline two: act on lead measures. A lag measure tells you whether you achieved the goal, such as revenue or audit findings, but by the time you see it, it is too late to change. A lead measure is predictive and influenceable: a behaviour that drives the goal and that the team can control, such as the number of client reviews completed each week. Discipline three: keep a compelling scoreboard, simple enough that anyone can see in five seconds whether the team is winning. People play differently when they keep score. Discipline four: create a cadence of accountability, a short weekly meeting in which each member reports on last week's commitments, reviews the scoreboard, and makes one or two new commitments for the coming week.
practice: Bossidy and Charan add that execution is the leader's most important job, not something to delegate. The leader must know the business, insist on realism, set clear priorities, follow through, and reward the doers. For anyone leading a strategy unit across several entities, the combination is practical: one or two wildly important goals per entity, lead measures you can track weekly, a visible scoreboard, and a fifteen-minute weekly accountability meeting that never gets cancelled.
faith: So when you have finished your duties, then stand up for worship, and to your Lord direct your longing. Mujahid and others explained it, as Ibn Kathir reports: when you finish your worldly work, turn to worship; when you finish one task, begin the next with effort. The verse describes a rhythm of continuous, directed effort, never idle, always aimed at Allah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught that the most beloved deeds are those done consistently even if small: a lead measure, practised weekly.
nigerian: The Yoruba say «Ọ̀rọ̀ púpọ̀ kì í kún agbọ̀n»: many words do not fill a basket. Nigeria has never lacked plans. Execution, with focus, measurement and follow-through, is what fills the basket.
practices: Choose one wildly important goal for the next quarter in the form 'from X to Y by date'.
Define two lead measures your team can control weekly.
Hold a 15-minute weekly accountability meeting for the next six weeks without cancelling it.
reflect: How many 'top priorities' do I really have?
Am I tracking only lag measures that tell me too late?
closing: When you finish one task, stand up for the next, and direct your longing to your Lord. Focus, measure, score and follow through.

verses.ar: فَإِذَا فَرَغْتَ فَٱنصَبْ
verses.en: So when you have finished [your duties], then stand up [for worship].

verses.ar: وَإِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ فَٱرْغَب
verses.en: And to your Lord direct [your] longing.

title: The Balanced Scorecard & OKRs
tag: What gets measured gets managed, so measure what truly matters.
source: Robert Kaplan and David Norton, 'The Balanced Scorecard', Harvard Business Review (1992); The Strategy-Focused Organization (2000); John Doerr, Measure What Matters (2018)
opening: In 1992 Robert Kaplan of Harvard Business School and the consultant David Norton argued that managing a company by financial numbers alone is like flying a plane with only one instrument. Their answer, the balanced scorecard, became one of the most widely adopted management tools in the world.
idea: Financial measures are lag indicators: they report the results of past actions. Kaplan and Norton proposed balancing them with three other perspectives. The customer perspective: how do customers see us? The internal process perspective: what must we excel at? And the learning and growth perspective: can we continue to improve and create value? Together, these four perspectives give a balanced view of performance and connect long-term strategy to short-term action. Their later work introduced strategy maps, diagrams that show the cause-and-effect chain: skilled and motivated people improve key processes, which delight customers, which produces financial results.
mechanics: A well-built scorecard has a small number of objectives in each perspective, each with a measure, a target and an initiative. The discipline is translating vague strategy into specific measures that people at every level understand. John Doerr, who learned the method from Andy Grove at Intel and brought it to Google, popularised a simpler cousin: objectives and key results. An objective is what you want to achieve, inspiring and qualitative. Key results are three to five measurable outcomes that show whether you got there. Doerr emphasises that OKRs should be ambitious, transparent across the organisation, and reviewed often. Grading them honestly, rather than hitting every target easily, is a sign of a healthy culture.
practice: Both tools carry a warning, often attributed to the economist Charles Goodhart: when a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure. People optimise the number and lose the purpose. The best accountability systems combine numbers with judgement, review the measures themselves regularly, and keep the cause-and-effect logic visible so people remember why each number matters.
faith: And every person We have fastened his record to his neck, and We will produce for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will find spread open. Read your record; sufficient is yourself against you this Day as an accountant. Every human life has a scorecard, recorded with perfect accuracy and balance across every dimension: worship, character, family, wealth and knowledge. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said, in a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi, that a servant's feet will not move on the Day of Resurrection until he is asked about his life and how he spent it, his knowledge and what he did with it, his wealth and how he earned and spent it, and his body and how he used it. Four perspectives, balanced.
nigerian: In public institutions across Nigeria, performance contracts and dashboards have often measured activity rather than outcomes: workshops held, not lives improved. A balanced scorecard asks the harder question at every level: is our work actually producing the results our stakeholders need?
practices: Draft one objective and three key results for your unit for next quarter.
Draw a simple strategy map: people, processes, stakeholders, results.
Use the hadith's four questions as a personal monthly scorecard: time, knowledge, wealth, body.
reflect: Which number in my work has become a target that distorts behaviour?
If my record were opened today, which perspective would be weakest?
closing: Measure what matters, balance the perspectives, and remember that the most important record of all is fastened to your own neck.

verses.ar: وَكُلَّ إِنسَٰنٍ أَلْزَمْنَٰهُ طَٰٓئِرَهُۥ فِى عُنُقِهِۦ وَنُخْرِجُ لَهُۥ يَوْمَ ٱلْقِيَٰمَةِ كِتَٰبًا يَلْقَىٰهُ مَنشُورًا
verses.en: And [for] every person We have imposed his fate upon his neck, and We will produce for him on the Day of Resurrection a record which he will encounter spread open.

verses.ar: ٱقْرَأْ كِتَٰبَكَ كَفَىٰ بِنَفْسِكَ ٱلْيَوْمَ عَلَيْكَ حَسِيبًا
verses.en: [It will be said], "Read your record. Sufficient is yourself against you this Day as accountant."

title: Thinking, Fast and Slow
tag: Your mind has two systems, and the fast one is in charge more often than you think.
source: Daniel Kahneman, Thinking, Fast and Slow (2011); Tversky and Kahneman, 'Judgment under Uncertainty: Heuristics and Biases', Science (1974)
opening: Daniel Kahneman was a psychologist who won the Nobel Prize in economics. With his partner Amos Tversky, he spent decades showing that human judgement fails in systematic, predictable ways. Their work changed economics, medicine, law and public policy.
idea: Kahneman describes two modes of thinking. System 1 is fast, automatic and intuitive: it reads faces, completes the phrase 'bread and', and jumps to conclusions effortlessly. System 2 is slow, deliberate and effortful: it does long division, checks an argument, and follows rules. We like to think System 2 is in charge. In reality, System 2 is lazy. It often accepts the quick story System 1 offers without checking. Most of our errors come not from stupidity but from trusting a fast impression where slow thought was needed.
mechanics: System 1 relies on heuristics, mental shortcuts that are usually useful but sometimes badly wrong. Anchoring: an initial number, even an irrelevant one, pulls later estimates towards it, which is why first offers matter in negotiation. Availability: we judge how likely something is by how easily examples come to mind, so vivid recent events feel more probable than they are. Loss aversion: losses hurt roughly twice as much as equivalent gains please, which makes people cling to failing projects. Overconfidence and the planning fallacy: we underestimate how long and how costly projects will be. And what Kahneman called WYSIATI, what you see is all there is: the mind builds a confident story from whatever information is in front of it, without asking what is missing.
practice: Kahneman was pessimistic about fixing biases in individuals. Even he, after a lifetime of study, admitted he still fell for them. His hope lay in organisations, which can build procedures that slow decisions down: checklists, independent assessments, and what he called the outside view, asking how similar projects have actually turned out instead of trusting the inside story of this one. A compliance review, an investment committee or an audit is, at its best, a deliberate System 2 for the whole organisation.
faith: O you who believe, if a wrongdoer comes to you with news, verify it, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and then become regretful over what you have done. Ibn Kathir records that the verse was revealed about a report that a tribe had refused to pay zakah, which turned out to be false. The Qur'an orders a System 2 pause precisely when emotion and a convincing story push us towards fast action. The scholars of hadith built an entire science, 'ilm al-rijal, on this principle: no report is accepted on its surface; its chain and its narrators must be checked.
nigerian: Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie's talk, The Danger of a Single Story, is WYSIATI in human terms: when we know one story about a people or a person, we mistake it for the whole truth. And the Hausa say «Rashin sani ya fi dare duhu»: not knowing is darker than the night.
practices: Before any important decision, write down what information you do not have.
When estimating time or cost, ask how long similar projects actually took, not how long this one should take.
When a report makes you angry, apply the verse: verify before you act.
reflect: Which recent judgement of mine was really a fast story I never checked?
Where in my work does an early number anchor everything that follows?
closing: Your fast mind is a gift, but not a judge. Slow down where it matters, verify what you hear, and ask what you cannot see.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوٓا۟ إِن جَآءَكُمْ فَاسِقٌۢ بِنَبَإٍ فَتَبَيَّنُوٓا۟ أَن تُصِيبُوا۟ قَوْمًۢا بِجَهَٰلَةٍ فَتُصْبِحُوا۟ عَلَىٰ مَا فَعَلْتُمْ نَٰدِمِينَ
verses.en: O you who have believed, if there comes to you a disobedient one with information, investigate, lest you harm a people out of ignorance and become, over what you have done, regretful.

title: Noise
tag: Two experts, same facts, different verdicts. That variability is a hidden cost.
source: Daniel Kahneman, Olivier Sibony and Cass R. Sunstein, Noise: A Flaw in Human Judgment (2021)
opening: Bias is when judgements are consistently wrong in one direction. In their final major book, Kahneman, the strategy professor Olivier Sibony and the Harvard law professor Cass Sunstein argued that there is a second, largely ignored error: noise.
idea: Noise is unwanted variability in judgements that should be identical. Two underwriters pricing the same insurance risk, two judges sentencing similar offenders, two doctors reading the same scan, two analysts rating the same credit: in a fair and competent system, their answers should be close. In study after study, the authors found they were far apart. In one insurance company, executives guessed that two underwriters would differ by about ten percent on the same case. The actual median difference was around fifty-five percent. Wherever there is judgement, there is noise, and usually more than anyone expects.
mechanics: The authors break noise into parts. Level noise: some judges are simply harsher than others on average. Pattern noise: each person has their own idiosyncratic reactions to particular kinds of cases. And occasion noise: the same person judges differently depending on mood, fatigue, weather, or what came just before. One study they discuss found that judges' rulings varied with factors as irrelevant as the time of day. The cure they propose is decision hygiene: procedures that reduce noise without needing to know its direction. Use structured criteria. Break a judgement into independent sub-assessments before combining them. Have several people judge independently before discussing, so that the loudest voice does not anchor the rest. Use relative scales, comparing cases with each other, instead of absolute ones. And where possible, use simple rules or models, which are noise-free by design.
practice: This is directly relevant to any compliance, credit or investment process. If two officers would rate the same client's risk differently, the institution has a fairness and a regulatory problem, even if neither is biased. A noise audit is simple: give several people the same set of real cases, collect their independent judgements, and measure the spread. The result is usually humbling, and it shows exactly where guidelines and checklists are needed.
faith: O you who believe, be persistently firm in justice, witnesses for Allah, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allah is more worthy of both, so follow not desire, lest you not be just. Justice in Islam is not only about intention. It is about consistency: the same standard for the rich and the poor, the relative and the stranger. Ibn Taymiyyah wrote that Allah supports the just state even if it is unbelieving, and does not support the unjust state even if it is Muslim. Noise is a quiet form of injustice, because similar people receive different treatment by chance.
nigerian: For institutions in Nigeria, where trust in official decisions is often low, consistency is credibility. A regulator, a bank or a fund manager that treats similar cases alike, and can show its criteria, earns a legitimacy that no press release can buy.
practices: Write a short checklist of criteria for one recurring judgement in your work, such as client risk rating.
On your next committee decision, collect independent written views before discussion begins.
Run a small noise audit: give three colleagues the same two cases and compare their ratings.
reflect: Would two people in my team reach the same decision on the same file?
Do I judge differently when I am tired, rushed or irritated?
closing: Be firm in justice, and make it consistent. Structure your judgements, and let fairness be designed, not left to chance.

verses.ar: يَٰٓأَيُّهَا ٱلَّذِينَ ءَامَنُوا۟ كُونُوا۟ قَوَّٰمِينَ بِٱلْقِسْطِ شُهَدَآءَ لِلَّهِ وَلَوْ عَلَىٰٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَوِ ٱلْوَٰلِدَيْنِ وَٱلْأَقْرَبِينَ إِن يَكُنْ غَنِيًّا أَوْ فَقِيرًا فَٱللَّهُ أَوْلَىٰ بِهِمَا فَلَا تَتَّبِعُوا۟ ٱلْهَوَىٰٓ أَن تَعْدِلُوا۟ وَإِن تَلْوُۥٓا۟ أَوْ تُعْرِضُوا۟ فَإِنَّ ٱللَّهَ كَانَ بِمَا تَعْمَلُونَ خَبِيرًا
verses.en: O you who have believed, be persistently standing firm in justice, witnesses for Allāh, even if it be against yourselves or parents and relatives. Whether one is rich or poor, Allāh is more worthy of both. So follow not [personal] inclination, lest you not be just. And if you distort [your testimony] or refuse [to give it], then indeed Allāh is ever, of what you do, Aware.

title: Superforecasting
tag: Ordinary people who think like foxes outpredict the experts.
source: Philip Tetlock, Expert Political Judgment (2005); Tetlock and Dan Gardner, Superforecasting: The Art and Science of Prediction (2015)
opening: For about twenty years, the psychologist Philip Tetlock collected tens of thousands of predictions from experts about politics and economics. His first finding was embarrassing: on average, the experts did little better than chance. His second finding was more hopeful.
idea: Some people predict far better than others, and the difference is not intelligence or credentials. It is how they think. Tetlock borrowed an image from the philosopher Isaiah Berlin: the hedgehog knows one big thing, and the fox knows many little things. Hedgehogs force every event into one grand theory and speak with great confidence. Foxes are sceptical of grand theories, gather information from many sources, think in probabilities, and change their minds when the evidence changes. Foxes forecast better. In a large tournament run by a United States intelligence research agency, Tetlock's team of volunteer 'superforecasters', ordinary people with this fox-like habit, beat professional analysts with access to classified information.
mechanics: Superforecasters share recognisable habits. They break big questions into smaller ones they can estimate. They start with the base rate, how often things like this usually happen, before adjusting for the details of the case. They express beliefs in precise probabilities, such as sixty-five percent, rather than vague words like 'possibly'. They update often, in small steps, as new information arrives, instead of either ignoring it or overreacting. And they keep score. Forecasts were measured with Brier scores, which reward accuracy and punish overconfidence. Tetlock found that keeping score, and reviewing what went wrong, is itself what makes people improve. Teams that debated respectfully did better than individuals.
practice: Most organisations never check their forecasts. Budgets, project timelines and risk assessments are made, and nobody later compares them with what actually happened. Tetlock's lesson for any strategy unit is to write predictions down with numbers and dates, and then review them honestly. Vague forecasts can never be wrong, which is exactly why they never improve.
faith: Indeed, Allah has knowledge of the Hour, sends down the rain, and knows what is in the wombs. No soul knows what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul knows in what land it will die. Ibn Kathir explains, citing the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari, that these are the five keys of the unseen which only Allah knows. This is the ultimate foundation for the humility of the fox. A believer plans, estimates and prepares, as Yusuf did for the seven years, but always says «in sha' Allah», because the future belongs to Allah alone. Overconfidence about tomorrow is a spiritual error as much as an analytical one.
nigerian: Hausa wisdom says «Abin da babba ya hango yana kwance, yaro ko ya hau rimi ba zai gani ba»: what an elder sees lying down, a child cannot see even from the top of a silk-cotton tree. Experience matters. But Tetlock adds a warning: experience only becomes foresight when you check your past predictions against what really happened.
practices: Write three predictions about your work for the next six months, each with a probability and a date.
Before estimating, ask: how often does this kind of thing usually happen?
When you change your mind on a matter, note why. That is a sign of good thinking, not weakness.
reflect: Am I more often a hedgehog or a fox?
Which of my past forecasts have I never checked?
closing: Plan with numbers, update with humility, keep score, and say «in sha' Allah». The unseen belongs to Allah; our duty is to think carefully about what He lets us see.

verses.ar: إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عِندَهُۥ عِلْمُ ٱلسَّاعَةِ وَيُنَزِّلُ ٱلْغَيْثَ وَيَعْلَمُ مَا فِى ٱلْأَرْحَامِ وَمَا تَدْرِى نَفْسٌ مَّاذَا تَكْسِبُ غَدًا وَمَا تَدْرِى نَفْسٌۢ بِأَىِّ أَرْضٍ تَمُوتُ إِنَّ ٱللَّهَ عَلِيمٌ خَبِيرٌۢ
verses.en: Indeed, Allāh [alone] has knowledge of the Hour and sends down the rain and knows what is in the wombs. And no soul perceives what it will earn tomorrow, and no soul perceives in what land it will die. Indeed, Allāh is Knowing and Aware.

title: Mental Models
tag: Build a latticework of big ideas, and learn to think backwards.
source: Charlie Munger, 'A Lesson on Elementary, Worldly Wisdom' (USC Business School, 1994); 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' (Harvard, 1995); Poor Charlie's Almanack (2005)
opening: Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett's partner at Berkshire Hathaway for decades, was famous less for any single investment than for the way he thought. In talks at business schools, including a famous lecture at Harvard on the psychology of human misjudgement, he described a method anyone can learn.
idea: Munger argued that you cannot really know anything if you just remember isolated facts. You need a latticework of mental models: the big ideas from the major disciplines, such as psychology, economics, mathematics, physics, biology and history, hung together so they support each other. Someone who knows only one discipline sees every problem through it; as the saying goes, to a man with a hammer, everything looks like a nail. With eighty or ninety important models, he said, you can handle most of the problems life brings. The goal is not cleverness. It is avoiding stupidity, consistently, over a long time.
mechanics: Several of his models have become classics. Inversion: borrowed from the mathematician Carl Jacobi, 'invert, always invert'. Instead of asking how to succeed, ask what would guarantee failure, and avoid it. Circle of competence: know the boundaries of what you truly understand, and stay inside them, or admit when you are outside. Incentives: never underestimate their power; if you want to predict behaviour, look at how people are paid. Second-order thinking: ask 'and then what?' about every decision. Margin of safety: leave room for error, because you will be wrong sometimes. And the combination of several psychological tendencies at once, which he called the lollapalooza effect, explains why groups sometimes behave in wildly irrational ways.
practice: Inversion is powerful in compliance and risk work. Instead of asking 'how do we stay compliant?', ask 'what would be the surest way to end up in front of the regulator?' The answers, such as poor records, unchecked conflicts of interest, silence about small breaches, become a precise list of controls. Munger's habit of reading widely, across fields, is also a discipline: he said he knew no wise person who did not read all the time.
faith: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart, about all of those one will be questioned. Ibn Kathir explains it as a prohibition on speaking or judging without knowledge, whether by suspicion or guesswork. This is the circle of competence as a religious duty. The classical scholars modelled the latticework too. Ibn Khaldun, in his Muqaddimah, combined history, economics, sociology and theology to explain how states rise and fall. Imam al-Shafi'i combined language, hadith and reason to found the science of usul al-fiqh.
nigerian: Nigeria's problems rarely respect disciplinary boundaries: an energy question is also a currency, security and politics question. A Nigerian leader with a latticework of models, faith, economics, history and the psychology of people, is equipped for problems a specialist cannot even see.
practices: For your current biggest decision, ask: what would guarantee failure? Then avoid those things.
Draw the boundary of your circle of competence, and name one decision this month that lies outside it.
Read one book outside your profession this quarter, and note one model it gives you.
reflect: What incentives are shaping the behaviour I am trying to change?
Where am I speaking with confidence outside my knowledge?
closing: Gather the big ideas, think backwards, stay inside what you know, and do not pursue what you have no knowledge of.

verses.ar: وَلَا تَقْفُ مَا لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهِۦ عِلْمٌ إِنَّ ٱلسَّمْعَ وَٱلْبَصَرَ وَٱلْفُؤَادَ كُلُّ أُو۟لَٰٓئِكَ كَانَ عَنْهُ مَسْـُٔولًا
verses.en: And do not pursue that of which you have no knowledge. Indeed, the hearing, the sight and the heart - about all those [one] will be questioned.

title: Thinking in Bets
tag: A good decision can have a bad outcome. Stop judging decisions by results alone.
source: Annie Duke, Thinking in Bets (2018); How to Decide (2020); Quit (2022)
opening: Annie Duke was a champion professional poker player who studied cognitive psychology at graduate level. Poker taught her something most executives never learn: you can play a hand perfectly and still lose, and play it badly and still win.
idea: Duke's central concept is 'resulting': judging the quality of a decision by the quality of its outcome. It is the most common error in organisational life. A manager who approved a sound investment that failed because of an unforeseeable event is blamed; a manager who took a reckless gamble that happened to work is promoted. Over time, resulting teaches people the wrong lessons. Duke argues that life is more like poker than chess. Chess has complete information and little luck. Life has hidden information and a great deal of luck. So every decision is a bet on an uncertain future, and should be judged by the quality of the thinking, the information and the options at the time it was made.
mechanics: Thinking in bets changes how you speak and decide. Instead of 'I'm sure', ask 'how sure, and what would I bet on it?' This simple question exposes overconfidence. Instead of reviewing only failures, review successes too, separating skill from luck in both. Duke recommends a 'decision group' of people committed to accuracy over comfort, who reward each other for honest self-assessment rather than for good outcomes. She also uses premortems: imagine the decision has failed a year from now, and list the reasons why. And she argues that quitting, at the right time, is a skill. Most people persist too long with failing projects because they cannot bear the sunk cost.
practice: For any committee or board, the lesson is to keep a record of why decisions were made: what was known, what was assumed, and what alternatives were considered. Then, when outcomes arrive, the decision can be evaluated fairly. This protects good decision-makers from being punished for bad luck, and stops the organisation from rewarding lucky recklessness.
faith: Perhaps you dislike a thing and it is good for you, and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. Allah knows, while you know not. This verse dissolves resulting at its root. The believer is accountable for his intention, his effort and his choice of means. The outcome belongs to Allah. The Prophet, peace be upon him, taught us istikharah for decisions, asking Allah to choose what is best, and taught that after taking the means, we rely on Him. If the result is not what we hoped, we say «qaddara Allah wa ma sha'a fa'al», Allah decreed and did what He willed, as in the hadith in Sahih Muslim, and we do not say 'if only'.
nigerian: In Nigeria's volatile environment, with sudden policy shifts and currency moves, good decisions often produce bad outcomes for reasons nobody could control. Leaders who judge their teams by the quality of decisions, not just results, build people who keep thinking clearly through the turbulence.
practices: For your next significant decision, write one paragraph: what I know, what I assume, and what I chose and why.
Run a premortem before launching a project: it failed, so why?
Pray istikharah for one important pending decision this week.
reflect: Have I blamed someone, including myself, for a good decision that met bad luck?
Which project am I continuing only because of what I have already spent on it?
closing: Judge the decision, not the dice. Think carefully, take the means, ask Allah to choose, and accept His decree with a calm heart.

verses.ar: كُتِبَ عَلَيْكُمُ ٱلْقِتَالُ وَهُوَ كُرْهٌ لَّكُمْ وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تَكْرَهُوا۟ شَيْـًٔا وَهُوَ خَيْرٌ لَّكُمْ وَعَسَىٰٓ أَن تُحِبُّوا۟ شَيْـًٔا وَهُوَ شَرٌّ لَّكُمْ وَٱللَّهُ يَعْلَمُ وَأَنتُمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَ
verses.en: Battle has been enjoined upon you while it is hateful to you. But perhaps you hate a thing and it is good for you; and perhaps you love a thing and it is bad for you. And Allāh knows, while you know not.

title: Black Swans & Antifragility
tag: Some things break under shocks, some survive them, and some grow stronger.
source: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, The Black Swan (2007); Antifragile (2012); Skin in the Game (2018)
opening: Nassim Nicholas Taleb, a former options trader turned philosopher of risk, spent his career attacking the false precision of financial models. The 2008 financial crisis, which most models said was nearly impossible, made his ideas famous.
idea: A Black Swan is an event that is rare, has extreme impact, and is explained afterwards as if it had been predictable. Wars, pandemics, crashes, a sudden currency collapse. Taleb argues that history is driven far more by these rare events than by the normal fluctuations our models measure. Since we cannot predict them, the right question is not 'what will happen?' but 'how exposed am I if something extreme happens?' This leads to his most important idea: antifragility. Fragile things break under stress, like a glass. Robust things resist stress, like a rock. But antifragile things gain from stress, disorder and volatility, like muscles that grow from exercise or an immune system strengthened by exposure.
mechanics: Taleb offers several practical principles. The barbell strategy: keep most of your resources extremely safe, and a small portion in high-upside experiments, avoiding the risky middle. Redundancy: keep reserves, savings and spare capacity, which look inefficient in normal times and save you in crises. Via negativa: improvement often comes more from removing harmful things, such as debt, bad habits or toxic relationships, than from adding new ones. Optionality: prefer positions with limited downside and open-ended upside. And skin in the game: never trust advice from people who do not bear the consequences of being wrong. Systems become fragile when those who take the risks are not the ones who pay for failures.
practice: For a fund manager or a compliance officer, Taleb's thinking challenges comfortable assumptions. A portfolio that performs well in normal years may hide a catastrophic exposure to one rare event. A company running at maximum efficiency with no cash buffer is fragile. Stress-testing, holding reserves, avoiding excessive leverage, and insisting that decision-makers share in the downside are the institutional forms of antifragility. Islamic finance's preference for risk-sharing over interest-based debt is, in Taleb's language, a principle of skin in the game.
faith: He entered his garden while wronging himself. He said: I do not think this will ever perish, and I do not think the Hour will ever come. The owner of the two gardens in Surah al-Kahf is the portrait of fragility: total confidence that the good years will last. One night, everything was destroyed. Yusuf, by contrast, built antifragility into Egypt: store in the seven good years for the seven hard ones. The Prophet, peace be upon him, told the man who asked whether to trust Allah or tie his camel: tie it, and trust in Allah, in a hadith recorded by al-Tirmidhi. Preparation and reliance on Allah belong together.
nigerian: The Yoruba say «Ilé ọba tó jó, ẹwà ló bù kún un»: when the king's palace burns, it is rebuilt more beautiful. That is antifragility in one line. Nigerian traders and families who survived repeated currency shocks often did so through Taleb's principles: diversified income, low debt, and networks of mutual support.
practices: List the three events that would hurt you or your organisation most, and one buffer for each.
Remove one fragility this month: a debt, a single point of failure, or a harmful habit.
Before taking advice, ask: does this person bear any cost if they are wrong?
reflect: Am I fragile, robust or antifragile in my finances, career and health?
Where am I acting like the owner of the garden, sure that the good times will last?
closing: You cannot predict the storm, but you can prepare for it. Tie your camel, store for the lean years, and trust in Allah.

verses.ar: وَدَخَلَ جَنَّتَهُۥ وَهُوَ ظَالِمٌ لِّنَفْسِهِۦ قَالَ مَآ أَظُنُّ أَن تَبِيدَ هَٰذِهِۦٓ أَبَدًا
verses.en: And he entered his garden while he was unjust to himself. He said, "I do not think that this will perish - ever.

verses.ar: وَمَآ أَظُنُّ ٱلسَّاعَةَ قَآئِمَةً وَلَئِن رُّدِدتُّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّى لَأَجِدَنَّ خَيْرًا مِّنْهَا مُنقَلَبًا
verses.en: And I do not think the Hour will occur. And even if I should be brought back to my Lord, I will surely find better than this as a return."
